clue.text: Cocaine bagged up — way over the top

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece set over the top of the next comes first

parts.note: S for south, a compass direction or way to go

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: to have bagged a prize is to have won it

explanation.surface: Drugs smuggled in bags are handled excessively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns WON into NOW; S, placed 'over the top' of it, comes first. The S as 'way' (south) is a loose convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow is long-standing street slang for powdered cocaine, from its white powdery look.

clue.text: Make love, live to be around 51 — grand!

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: the verb phrase tells us one piece goes round the others

parts.note: to live is to be, to exist
LI is 51 in Roman numerals
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: A romantic urge to live past fifty and have a thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be around' is the container signal: the being-around piece wraps the Roman numeral and the grand. 'Make' looks like 'make love' but stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To oblige someone can mean to compel them, so it is a synonym of make in that forcing sense.

clue.text: Impervious to RAF power ground

indicators.note: ground means crushed and broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pilot boasts that the air force's might cannot be stopped by any foe on the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' reshuffles the ten letters of TO RAF POWER.
explanation.definitionFit: Something impervious lets nothing through, and waterproof material keeps out rain in just that way.

clue.text: Tending to react to irritating feature in snitch

definitions.text: Tending to react to irritating feature in snitch

parts.words: Tending to react to irritating feature in snitch
parts.note: snitch is slang for the nose, and the irritating thing in it makes one prone to an involuntary blast

explanation.surface: Someone who reacts badly to an annoying informer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snitch' looks like an informer, but here it is the nose. The answer is also one of Snow White's seven dwarfs, a theme of this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Being given to fits of the nose's explosive reflex when it is tickled describes this adjective exactly.

clue.text: Freud-like, say, sit it out in electrical discharge

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: an arc is a luminous discharge of electricity across a gap

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: A psychoanalyst sits out a session during a power surge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the fodder and 'in' sets it inside the discharge. Freud here is Lucian Freud the painter, not Sigmund the analyst; 'say' marks him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucian Freud was a painter, so being like him is an example of having a creative, painterly character.

clue.text: Christmas solvers will vociferously change the written word "heavenwards"

indicators.note: said out loud, so the phrase's sound counts rather than its spelling

parts.note: solvers are you, so solvers will is you will, contracted

indicators.note: in a down clue, upwards means read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: to edit is to alter written text

explanation.surface: Solvers protest at a festive rewording of a hymn's 'heavenwards'.
explanation.walkthrough: The contraction of 'you will' sounds like YULE; 'heavenwards' turns EDIT into TIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuletide is the old name for the Christmas season, from the Norse midwinter feast.

clue.text: Brandished cape with wave

indicators.note: brandished means waved about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone flourished a cape and waved it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brandished' scrambles CAPE WITH.
explanation.definitionFit: A whitecap is a wave whose crest breaks into white foam.

clue.text: Political loyalist gets straight down

parts.note: true means straight, as in a true line
blue means sad or down

explanation.surface: A party loyalist goes straight down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets' joins the definition to the wordplay. Blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A true blue is a staunch, unwavering supporter, especially of the British Conservatives.

clue.text: Hardly rocket science, underwear lacking rein for adjustment

parts.note: lacking underwear is having no bra

indicators.note: something needing adjustment must be reset, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Underwear without the strap needing adjustment is easy to understand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for adjustment' rearranges the rein's letters, which follow the underwear-less phrase. Rocket science is the stock example of something hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-brainer is a task or choice needing no thought, the opposite of something complex like rocket science.

clue.text: An official guide to seating

parts.note: a person employed to show people to their places at a theatre or wedding

explanation.definitionFit: Showing guests to their seats is the main job of this attendant at a theatre or wedding.

clue.text: Bit end of pie/pasty

parts.note: a whit is a tiny bit, as in not a whit

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A bit from the end of a pie or pasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pasty' looks like the pie but is the adjective meaning pale.
explanation.definitionFit: A pasty face is pale and colourless, which is a looser sense of the colour white.

clue.text: Beowulf-like, enter rocky point above the source of upheaval

definitions.text: point above the source of upheaval

parts.note: Beowulf is an Old English epic poem

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady, so the letters are shaken up

explanation.surface: An epic hero enters rocky ground above a cataclysm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocky' turns ENTER into ENTRE.
explanation.definitionFit: In an earthquake, the epicentre is the surface point directly above the focus underground.

clue.text: River circling once fashionable isle

indicators.note: one word goes round another

parts.note: the Spey is a Scottish river
hep is a dated word for hip or trendy

explanation.surface: A river surrounds a once trendy island.
explanation.walkthrough: SPEY goes 'circling' HEP. The Spey is a Scottish salmon river; the Isle of Sheppey is in Kent, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheppey is an island off the north Kent coast in the Thames estuary.

clue.text: Title: "Henry Enters Bent Over"

indicators.note: one piece goes in another
in a down clue, over means turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: a bent is a natural leaning or bias
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A headline about a man named Henry coming in stooped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' turns BIAS into SAIB, and H 'Enters' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sahib was a respectful form of address in colonial India, like 'sir'.

clue.text: Level unit releasing large bird of prey

parts.note: a tier is a level or row

indicators.note: releasing means letting go, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a cell is a basic unit, as in biology or a political cell
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A tidy unit sets a large raptor free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'releasing' drops an L from CELL, leaving CEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiercel is a male hawk, especially a peregrine falcon, used in falconry.

clue.text: Former wife Henry VIII beheaded: country gives a sigh

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse
Henry VIII was nicknamed Bluff King Hal

indicators.note: beheaded removes the first letter of the word that follows

parts.note: a nation is a country

explanation.surface: A history-book note about Henry VIII's executed queen, then a country's sigh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' looks like it applies to the wife, as in Anne Boleyn, but it takes the first letter off NATION.
explanation.definitionFit: An exhalation is a breath out, and a sigh is one such long, audible breath.

clue.text: Crossword setter's hen party ending in physical upheaval

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other
in a down clue, heaving up reads the word from bottom to top

parts.note: real, as opposed to imaginary, means physical

indicators.note: ending picks the final letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A setter's party for hens ends in a physical brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upheaval' turns REAL into LAER and the last letter of 'party' goes 'in'. Setters often use 'layer' for a hen, a classic red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen is an egg layer, a word crossword setters use often to mislead.

clue.text: Anything put in house, like a teach-yourself guide

indicators.note: one piece is placed within another

parts.note: owt is northern English dialect for anything

explanation.surface: Anything placed in a home, such as a DIY manual.
explanation.walkthrough: OWT is 'put in' HO. Owt is used in northern England ('owt or nowt', anything or nothing).
explanation.definitionFit: A how-to is a practical instruction guide for learning a task by yourself.

clue.text: Car cleaning mechanism happened to be hot with current applied to power energy

parts.note: was is the past tense of be
H is the tap abbreviation for hot
I is the physics symbol for electric current
P is the symbol for power
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A car-wash gadget that was hot, with current applied to give it power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'applied to' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A wash-wipe is the windscreen washer and wiper system on a car, spraying and sweeping the glass.

clue.text: Recording over gulping duck's "quack"

indicators.note: gulping means swallowing, so one piece takes another inside
over means turned over, read backwards

parts.note: a CD is a compact disc recording
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, the letter O

explanation.surface: A recording of a duck's call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns CD into DC, which goes 'gulping' O. 'quack' is a fake doctor, not the duck's noise; a duck is a zero score in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Doc is an informal word for doctor, and quack is a slang term for doctor too.

clue.text: When forced, admit harbouring man by a coastal strip of land

indicators.note: harbouring means sheltering, so one piece holds another
forced means wrenched into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Al is a man's name

explanation.surface: When pressed, someone admits sheltering a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When forced' rearranges the fodder into DMATI, 'harbouring' takes the man inside after its first letter, and 'by' joins the final A.
explanation.definitionFit: Dalmatia is the coastal region of Croatia along the Adriatic, a long narrow strip of land.

clue.text: Jolly unpleasant woman has Rex yielding to pressure

indicators.note: one letter gives way to another, so it is replaced

parts.note: a harpy is a grasping, unpleasant woman
R stands for Rex, king
P is the symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: A cheerful nag whose king gives way under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: In HARPY, R 'yielding to' P gives the answer. Rex is Latin for king, as in royal signatures.
explanation.definitionFit: Being jolly is being cheerful and merry, a close synonym of glad.

clue.text: Given to retirement party almost lacking space

parts.note: a bash is a party

indicators.note: almost removes the last letter of a word

parts.note: something full has no space left

explanation.surface: A retirement party nearly too crowded for room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retirement' is not leaving work but being retiring, shy. 'almost' trims FULL to FUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Being given to retiring, keeping back from others, means being shy.

clue.text: Stone artist's classic

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight
Fernand Leger was a French painter; the 's means is

explanation.surface: A stone sculptor's masterpiece.
explanation.walkthrough: The St Leger at Doncaster is one of Britain's five classic flat horse races; a stone is a British weight of 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The classics are the five main British flat races, and the St Leger is the oldest.

clue.text: Rather drippy, grabbing top of ledge, ready to drop off

indicators.note: grabbing means holding, so one piece is put inside another

parts.note: seepy means leaking a little

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A drippy person clinging to a ledge, about to fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drop off' looks like falling from the ledge, but it means falling asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling ready to drop off to sleep is being drowsy.

clue.text: Cross borne by George Smiley, extremely protective of back

indicators.note: being protective of something is to enclose it
the extremes of a phrase are its first and last letters

parts.note: the rump is the hind part or back

explanation.surface: George Smiley bears a cross, extremely protective of his back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'borne by' only joins. George Smiley is John le Carre's spymaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Being cross is being annoyed, short-tempered.

clue.text: Perhaps oily street scene trader initially has Superman accessory

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of a word

parts.note: to own something is to have it
Superman wears a red cape

explanation.surface: A trader keeps a Superman cape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oily' means an oil painting; 'Perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A townscape is a painting or view of a town, and an oil painting could be one.

clue.text: See 6
Bean-type, say, falling about, having a ball

indicators.note: having means containing, so one piece holds another
falling about suggests a jumble, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: O looks like a ball

explanation.surface: A bean-like person laughing at a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falling about' turns SAY into SYA, and 'having' places O inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Soya is a bean grown for food and oil, so a kind of bean.

clue.text: Tom very low, seeing Buzz in grip of bacterial disease

indicators.note: one piece is held inside another

parts.note: TB is tuberculosis
a hum is a low buzz

explanation.surface: A depressed Tom finds a buzzing sound in a sick person.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Thumb is a tiny folk-tale hero, so 'very low' (short) completes the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Thumb is a famously tiny hero of English folk tale, so short in stature.

clue.text: See 8
"Dense grass by ditches black!"

parts.note: dope is slang for cannabis, which is also slang grass

indicators.note: ditches means drops or abandons, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: B is the pencil abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: Thick grass beside ditches turned black.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ditches' looks like trenches but means drops: BY loses B.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dense is being stupid, and dopey is a slang term for slow-witted.

clue.text: Early arrival's announcement before start of untitled short musical piece

parts.note: an early arrival might announce I'm prompt

indicators.note: start of takes the first letter of a word

explanation.surface: Someone arrives early and announces a short untitled tune.
explanation.definitionFit: An impromptu is a short piece of music, often for piano, with an improvised feel.
